posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
> After IPA my holo disappeared and no hot-drying helped.What screwed up ?

If you put the plate back into the IPA, I think it needs to go through the swelling bath again first. The reason your holo's are so blue is because of a slight error in the concentrations in my formula. I will adjust it in the Wiki now. Because of the added Boric Acid and reduced quantity of gelatin, more shrinkage happens than in the original Jeff Blyth formula.

With the updated formula in the Wiki (after 5 minutes from now), you will get bright green/yellow holograms.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
Here is the predicted replay wavelength when using the new formula:

- We have 12 g gelatin.

- The weight of the chemicals is calculated as follows:

--- 4,8ml TMG x 25% = about 1.2g

--- .77g Boric Acid = .77g

--- 1ml Potassium Chromate (at 5%)= .05g

--- 6ml MB at 0.4% = .024g

--- Total weight of chemicals: 2g

- This is 17% of the weight of the gelatin. Thus the gelatin should shrink about 17% after exposed and these chemicals are washed out.

- A hologram recorded with a laser diode at 650nm will then replay at (1-.17)*650 = 540nm

These calculations are not super accurate, but adequate for our work. I have confirmed this formula by making a hologram with these concentrations and then measuring the replay wavelength with a cheap spectrophotometer from ProjectStar. (In my humble opinion a valuable instrument that every holographer could use).

posts.author: Cristiano_Perrucci
posts.content_md:
> **Hans:** After IPA my holo disappeared and no hot-drying helped.What screwed up ?If you put the plate back into the IPA, I think it needs to go through the swelling bath again first.

I reprocess my dim or spotted holos putting developed plates (@ room temp) into cold tap water (~15C) until emulsion is soaked. Than I put plates into IPA baths as usual.

Before developing plates, I check water concentration of IPA baths with a alcholometer. It costs 3.7 euro at the local hard store.

I've also done some of observations varing the rate water/IPA:

GREEN DIM NARROWBAND HOLOS

1st bath: 50/50 water/IPA

2nd bath: 20/80 water/IPA

3rd bath: 100 IPA

GOLD/ORANGE BRIGHT (supernova like) BROADBAND HOLOS

1st bath: 10/90 water/IPA

2nd bath: 100 IPA

while:

SPOTTED (green and blue spotted) HOLOS 

1st bath: 40/60 water/IPA

2nd bath: 30/70 water/IPA

3rd bath: 20/80 water/IPA

4th bath: 10/90 water/IPA

5th bath: 100 IPA

Best replay at longer wavelength (toward the red) has been made reducing TMG acetate. But in this case plates sensitivity decreases.

> Could you please tell me a bit more about this, as I would like to get one.

It is a glass part that looks like a float (like one uses when float fishing). It has a scale on the side. You can drop it in a vertical container with the alcohol mix and then read on the scale how deep it has sunk in the mixture. The scale will then indicate the concentration of the IPA.

I think it can be easily made in the kitchen lab witha thin straw that is closed on both ends and weighted down on one end. Then drop it in 100% IPA and place a mark with a pen or make a little scratch at the IPA level on the straw. Next, drop it into say 70% IPA and place another mark. You can do this for all your IPA solutions and always be sure they are at the right concentration with this little tool.

Joe, I too use an Alcohol Hydrometer which is intended for use in drinking alcohols. I think it was Colin that suggested it years ago and I find it very usefull. What I like best about having one is the amount of alcohol I save. 

Let's say I have 35%, 70%, 90% and 100% baths. After using them they become more saturated with water. So intead of throwing them all away I filter them through a coffee filter and then, using the alcohol hydrometer, dilute the watered down 100% to get my fresh 90%, I dilute the watered down 90% to get my 70% etc. Thus I usually only have to discard the watered down least concentrated bath.

Also, it just so happens that store bought over the counter alcohol comes in 70% (good for 35% and 70% baths) and 90%. But the 100% I have to order.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
> Can these calculations be taken as rule?

With MBDCG, I think so yes. It is an entirely different matter with classical DCG because there the hardening there takes place in a liquid (swollen state with hardening fix where the swelling seems to depend on the temperature of that bath). This may also explain why it is near to impossible to change the re-play colour of an MBDCG with different times in "tuning" baths.

> Does shrinking take place only after alcohol escapes from fringes?

I believe that is the case. I think two things take place here. Firstly, the alcohol takes the water out of the gelatin matrix. Secondly, the alohol stiffens the gelatin. If you start with a low concentration alcohol, the gelatin stiffens enough to prevent further deformation during the higher concentration baths. So, starting with a low concentration enables a narrow band hologram.

Also, when you start with a low concentration, the calculation of replay colour seems very accurate for my adapted MBDCG formula and for Jeff's original formula. 

If you start with a very high concentration of alcohol, the gelatin stiffens while the alcohol is extracting water from the gelatin. Water is able to escape more quickly at the surface of the gelatin and the gelatin stiffens as a whole throughout the thickness. This creates a differential shrinking throughout the thickness of the gelatin. The result is a broadband hologram. The same effect can be reached with a warmer water bath. The gelatin is then able to hold more water before it is thrown in the first alcohol bath.

> I shoot some holograms that appears pretty bright when plate is still wet after alcohol bath, but image disappears when alcohol escapes from fringes, and no further thermal processing restores image.

I think this might be because your alcohol is not 100%. The result is perhaps that while the plate is in that bath, there is some equilibrium. The alcohol has stiffened the gelatin, and at the same time, the water that is still there between the fringes holds the distance between the fringes. But where there is still water, the gelatin is not completely stiffened yet. As you remove the plate from that bath, the water evaporates and the fringes collapse. The plate will change colour from it's original green/yellow to blue/violet and disappear.

But perhaps this will work:

Process your plate in baths of normal alcohol of concentrations of 30% and 90%. Then, as the last bath, use pure acetone to remove the last bit of water and stiffen the gelatin more. It's a wild guess, but perhaps this will work for you.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
> **Hans:** Then, as the last bath, use pure acetone

The use of acetone in connection with DCG is interesting. There seems to be surprising lack of documentation regarding its use with gelatin.

I believe that acetone has a tanning effect on proteins in general, including gelatin. (It's soluble in water, but I don't know about alcohol.)

In the light of John's theory and successful experiment in red-shifting DCG with post-processing hardening by use of dichromate and light-exposure, I've been thinking about the possibilities of using a different hardening method, by chemical means only. To me, John's idea that the expanded fringes are "encouraged" to remain in an expanded state due to extra hardening (while swollen) is quite plausible, and very interesting. Maybe acetone could be used in this connection in the final bath, either alone or possibly with IPA (if the two are miscible, which I don't know). Supposedly, there is another form of acetone called dihydroxyacetone which is definitely soluble in water and alcohol.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Off Topic - 

A famous guitar manufacture had a process that melted plastic (acetate) in acetone to make a glue for the plastic. They had a large vat of acetone about 1 meter square and 10cm deep open all day on the production floor.

One day a fire marshal was walking through to inspect. He suddenly turned white and walked out the door. He went down the street and called the manufacture and told them to shut down the plant and evacuate immediately when the had to bring a cleanup team to keep the plant from catching fire.

Acetone not only has a low B.P. but the flames are so faint that it can be difficult to see the fire.
